---
title: "4A. Community differences (track A: insects)"
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

*Analyse differences in community composition between samples — beta diversity — using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).*

### Select samples

We keep the rows of the long table that belong to the samples selected in [step 3](insects-03-map.qmd). `semi_join()` filters one table by another, and DuckDB does the work without reading the whole table into R:

```r
selected <- duckdb_tibble(eventID = samples$eventID, .prudence = "stingy")
counts_selected <- merged$counts |> semi_join(selected, by = "eventID")
```

### Aggregate ASVs to clusters

In addition to ASV taxonomy and BOLD BINs, the IBA data also include project-specific cluster assignments in the `associatedSequences` column. Most pairs of samples share few ASVs, so comparing them at ASV level says rather little. We therefore sum the reads of each cluster in each sample, which in a long table is a join followed by a grouped sum.

The cluster assignments are read from `loaded`, because `merge_long()` keeps only the attributes that describe the ASV itself, and `associatedSequences` is specific to each dataset:

```r
clusters <- loaded$asvs |> distinct(taxonID, cluster = associatedSequences)

cluster_counts <- counts_selected |>
  inner_join(clusters, by = "taxonID") |>
  summarise(quant = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(eventID, cluster)) |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = cluster, quant)
```

The new names, `sample`, `taxon` and `quant`, are the ones that [`ecolongr`](https://github.com/biodiversitydata-se/ecolongr){target="_blank"} expects by default. Nothing has been computed yet: `cluster_counts` is still a query.

### Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity compares the abundances of taxa in two samples, from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities with nothing in common. We first turn the counts into relative abundances, so that sequencing depth does not affect the comparison, and then calculate the dissimilarities:

```r
bray <- cluster_counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = samples$eventID)
```

`el_decostand()` and `el_vegdist()` work like `decostand()` and `vegdist()` in the `vegan` package, but on the long table. `samples =` makes the result follow the order of the rows in `samples`, which we rely on when plotting. The result is an ordinary `dist` object, with one value per pair of samples, that `vegan` and base R can use.

### Run PCoA

Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) represents the dissimilarities among samples in a smaller number of dimensions:

```r
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)
```

Unlike the distances, PCoA needs the full matrix of dissimilarities in memory, and its run time grows quickly with the number of samples. That is fine for the samples we use here, but for many thousands of samples you may prefer `el_rda()`, a PCA that runs directly on the long table.

### Prepare colour scales

`habitat_cols` was already created in [step 3](insects-03-map.qmd). We add continuous colour scales for sampling date and latitude, plus colours for the two extraction methods:

```r
ramp <- colorRampPalette(rev(c(
  "#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE090", "#FFFFBF", "#E0F3F8", "#91BFDB", "#4575B4"
)))

yday_range <- min(samples$yday):max(samples$yday)
color_yday <- ramp(length(yday_range))
yday_index <- samples$yday - min(yday_range) + 1

lat_range <- floor(min(samples$decimalLatitude)):ceiling(max(samples$decimalLatitude))
color_lat <- ramp(length(lat_range))
lat_index <- round(samples$decimalLatitude) - min(lat_range) + 1

method_cols <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "#e76f51",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "#2a9d8f"
)
method_labs <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "homogenate",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "lysate"
)
```

For the legends, latitude is shown at 2-degree intervals and sampling date by month:

```r
lat_ticks <- seq(ceiling(min(lat_range) / 2) * 2, max(lat_range), by = 2)

month_ticks  <- sort(tapply(samples$yday, samples$month, min))
month_labels <- month.abb[as.integer(names(month_ticks))]
```

### Plot PCoA results

We plot the same PCoA four times, colouring samples by sampling date, habitat, latitude and extraction method:

```r
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 6), xpd = TRUE)

  # Panel: colour by year-day
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_yday[yday_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by year-day")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_yday[month_ticks - min(yday_range) + 1],
         legend = month_labels)

  # Panel: colour by habitat
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = habitat_cols[samples$habitat], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by habitat")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = habitat_cols, legend = names(habitat_cols))

  # Panel: colour by latitude
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_lat[lat_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by latitude")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_lat[lat_ticks - min(lat_range) + 1],
         legend = lat_ticks)

  # Panel: colour by extraction method
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = method_cols[samples$method], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by extraction method")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = method_cols, legend = method_labs)
}

plot_pcoa()
```

The first two PCoA axes explain only about 10% of the variation together, so the plots capture only part of the community differences. Even so, they suggest effects of sampling date, latitude and habitat: northern samples gather in one direction, forest samples spread out along the first axis, and spring samples form a tail of their own. Homogenate and lysate samples overlap in most of the plot, but they are not fully mixed. The spring tail, for example, consists mainly of homogenate samples.
